reasoning: The two best performers were 'What happens to your body without sleep' (reach 104) and 'Your memories change every time you recall them' (94). Both are Reels with a body or brain mechanism that applies to every viewer. The last six posts were all human body topics, so I'm moving to a close but fresh psychology and memory subject: infantile amnesia. It is universal, counterintuitive and drives comments ('what's your earliest memory?'). I'm keeping the Reel format with 5 slides, short texts and lofi music, since lofi was on the 104-reach post, plus palette 1, which was also on that post. This reel tests hook version B from the hook experiment: a direct claim or question about the reader instead of a bold number. It runs as a Trial Reel to start testing trial distribution, since nearly all reach is non-follower anyway. The caption ends with a personal-memory question to test comment-driving prompts after save and share prompts earned nothing.
topic: Infantile amnesia: why we can't remember being a baby
hook: Why you can't remember being a baby

slides.title: It has a name
slides.body: Scientists call it infantile amnesia. Most adults' earliest memories date back to around age 3.
slides.image_prompt: An empty wooden baby crib in a softly lit nursery, a tiny knitted blanket fading into mist, dreamy nostalgic atmosphere

slides.title: Babies do remember
slides.body: A 2025 Yale brain-scan study found 1-year-olds already storing new memories in the hippocampus.
slides.image_prompt: A small glowing seahorse-shaped structure inside a translucent brain model, soft blue light, floating baby toys around it
slides.credit: Raymond F Sekula Jr, Peter J Jannetta, Kenneth F Casey, Edward M Marchan, L Kath (CC BY 2.0) via wikimedia

slides.title: Kids forget later
slides.body: Kids aged 5 to 7 recall over 60% of events from age 3. By age 8 or 9, it drops to about 35%.
slides.image_prompt: A stack of faded childhood polaroid photos slowly dissolving into dust at the edges, warm vintage light on a wooden table

slides.title: Too many new neurons
slides.body: In young mice, a burst of new brain cells in the hippocampus wiped out early memories. Babies may be similar.
slides.image_prompt: Dense glowing neuron network growing rapidly, new branches covering older faint connections, deep blue and purple tones
slides.credit: ZEISS Microscopy from Germany (CC BY 2.0) via wikimedia

slides.title: Locked, not deleted?
slides.body: Scientists brought back 'forgotten' infant memories in mice using light. Yours may still be in there.
slides.image_prompt: An old brass key glowing with a beam of light, resting beside a locked tiny wooden memory box, dark moody background

cta: Follow for facts your brain forgets
caption:
Your brain was recording from your very first year. A 2025 Yale study scanned babies and found their hippocampus already storing new memories. So why can almost none of us remember being a baby?

One leading theory: the infant brain grows new neurons so fast that old memory links get scrambled. In mice, scientists even brought 'lost' infant memories back using light. So yours may still be in there somewhere.

What's your earliest memory, and how old were you? 👇
